summary: Lists the requirements for a new tool that IETF working group chairs and Area Directors could use to create and update working group charter milestones. It is meant as input to a later design and development effort and updates RFC 6292. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A club needs a to-do list for its goals. This writes down what features such a list tool would need for IETF groups, before anyone builds it.

subtitle: What IETF chairs and Area Directors would need from a tool that creates and updates working group milestones.

tldr.problem: Working group milestones are created and updated by hand: chairs email their Area Director or the Secretariat, who then makes the change.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements for a tool where chairs and Area Directors edit milestones directly, with approval rules, links to Internet-Drafts, reminders and a visible change history.
tldr.outcome: It is input for a later design and development effort, not a design itself, and it updates RFC 6292.

today: RFC 6433 is an Informational document that updates RFC 6292, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It states requirements only, as input to a later design and development effort.

sections.title: Why a Milestones Tool
sections.content:
Every IETF working group (WG) has milestones, such as publishing a particular Internet-Draft or starting discussion of a topic. They are one part of the WG charter. Changing milestones needs Area Director (AD) approval, while changing the charter text needs IESG approval.

Today the Secretariat does this work manually. WG chairs normally email their AD to ask for a change, and email the AD or the Secretariat when a milestone has been met. The IAOC asked for this document so that it could later be used to issue a request for proposals for the tool.

The tool must only touch the milestones of the current charter. The Datatracker keeps two sets, one for the current charter and one for a proposed recharter, and this tool must not change the second.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now, to change the goal list you have to write a letter to one person who edits it for you. The idea is to let the right people edit it themselves.

sections.title: Who Can Use the Tool and What They Can Change
sections.content:
Only WG chairs and ADs may use the tool. It reuses the login and access control from the tool described in RFC 6292. A person who chairs several WGs must be able to use the tool for all of them.

Any AD can add or update any milestone for any WG, though normally an AD works on their own WGs. This lets one AD cover for another. Chairs can only change milestones for their own WGs. The Secretariat must be able to do the same things as ADs, for fixing problems or making emergency changes.

A chair needs to see all milestones for the WG, change the due date, finished date, associated Internet-Drafts and description, delete milestones, and add new ones. The database records the date and the person behind every addition or change, and the community can see this.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the group leaders and the area bosses get to edit the list, and everyone can see who changed what and when.

sections.title: Which Changes Need Approval
sections.content:
The RFC names six actions: create milestones, delete milestones, change descriptions, change due dates, change which Internet-Drafts are associated, and assert that a milestone is no longer due. The tool must also support reordering the list.

Chairs can change due dates, change associated drafts, mark a milestone as no longer due, and reorder the list. These take effect immediately in the Datatracker, with an email to the AD and the chairs and no approval needed.

Creating, deleting and changing the description of a milestone are also open to chairs, but they do not show in the Datatracker until an AD approves them. The chair or AD must be able to review the proposed change before committing it. The tool must list pending changes for ADs and the Secretariat, sorted by the responsible AD.

When a milestone is marked no longer due, an arbitrary short phrase is given, often Done but possibly On hold. The only meaning the Datatracker attaches to it is that the milestone is no longer due. Once a day the Datatracker sends the WG one message listing the changes from the past 24 hours.
sections.plainLanguage: Small changes, like moving a date, happen right away. Bigger changes, like adding or deleting a goal, wait until a boss says yes.

sections.title: Linking Milestones to Internet-Drafts
sections.content:
There is currently no mechanism to map milestones to Internet-Drafts. Most milestones map to one draft, some map to none (for example, when a general discussion will begin), some map to several, and some drafts belong to more than one milestone.

The new tool must make this mapping explicit and list the drafts in views of the milestone. That needs a change to the Datatracker database. When a mapped draft moves to the state "Submitted to IESG for Publication" (see RFC 6174), the tool sends a message to the chairs as a reminder. They decide what to do, since the message does not apply to every mapped draft.
sections.plainLanguage: Each goal should say which papers it is about, so people can find them. Some goals have no paper, and some have several.

sections.title: Reminders and Viewing Changes
sections.content:
If an AD has not approved or rejected a pending request within a week, an email goes to the chairs and the AD, and repeats every week until the AD acts. Chairs also get reminders when a milestone is one month from due, when it is due, and every month it is overdue. For mapped drafts, they get a message one month before the draft expires and when it expires, and weekly mail while a milestone maps to an expired draft.

For the community, the RFC updates the requirements of RFC 6292. Search must cover any text in a milestone description and the names of mapped drafts. A new view must compare two full sets of milestones with differences highlighted and show who made each change. An Atom feed (RFC 4287) must report changes to a WG's milestones.

The security section says that a new milestones tool does not affect the security of the Internet in any significant fashion.
sections.plainLanguage: The tool nags the leaders when a goal is nearly due, late, or when a boss has not answered. Anyone can look at the history of changes.
